metadata.title: How stress predicts work engagement among primary and secondary school teachers: The mediating role of emotional labor and burnout, and the moderating role of school support

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used a stratified sample of 5,400 primary and secondary school teachers in China, with strata defined by teachers’ schools (school location and teaching period) and personal characteristics (gender and teaching years), and teaching period divided into elementary, junior high, and senior high. The manuscript does not report the use of any complex survey weights (e.g., sampling/design weights) or replicate-weight procedures, and it analyzes the data using structural equation modeling in SPSS/AMOS/Mplus rather than ILSA-style PV-based achievement estimation. Because no weight variable name is provided and no weighting strategy is described, the analysis appears to treat the retained sample as the analytic dataset without population-representative reweighting. Data preparation included excluding respondents based on response time thresholds, excluding vocational high school teachers, excluding schools categorized as “other,” excluding retired teachers, and excluding provinces/districts/cities with fewer than 10 respondents.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This study does not use ILSA cognitive achievement outcomes with Plausible Values; instead, it models teacher stress, emotional labor, burnout, work engagement, and school support measured via Likert-type questionnaires. Because the dependent variables are non-PV constructs, PV handling is not applicable. The manuscript also does not describe any missing-data handling procedure (e.g., imputation or deletion rules), so missing-data handling is treated as not reported rather than inferred.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: A stratified sample was drawn from China targeting primary and secondary school teachers (strata based on school location and teaching period, and personal characteristics such as gender and teaching years; teaching period divided into elementary, junior high, and senior high). From the initial stratified sample, respondents were excluded if they answered in less than 180 seconds or more than 10,000 seconds, if they came from vocational high schools, if their schools were categorized as “other,” if they were retired, and if the province/district/city had fewer than 10 total respondents. After exclusions, 5,400 participants were retained (effective sample rate 94.13%).

main_findings.dataset_used: Teacher questionnaire survey (China; primary & secondary teachers)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Structural equation model fit: CFI=0.842, RMSEA=0.084, PNFI=0.774. Direct effect: teacher stress → work engagement β=-0.316 (p<.01). Mediation: teacher stress → burnout → work engagement indirect βindirect=-0.247 (p<.01); teacher stress → surface acting → burnout → work engagement indirect βindirect=-0.038 (p<.01); teacher stress → expression of naturally felt emotions → work engagement indirect βindirect=0.011 (p<.05); teacher stress → deep acting → work engagement indirect βindirect=0.011 (p<.05); teacher stress → surface acting → work engagement indirect βindirect=-0.076 (p<.01).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the China primary-and-secondary teacher questionnaire survey the study leveraged teacher stress and emotional-labor/burnout pathways (surface acting, deep acting, expression of naturally felt emotions, and burnout) to predict work engagement, finding that teacher stress had a significant negative direct effect on work engagement (β=-0.316, p<.01) and that burnout and surface acting pathways mediated additional negative effects. This indicates that reducing teacher stress and limiting maladaptive emotional labor (especially surface acting) may strengthen teachers’ work engagement, though the cross-sectional self-report design limits causal interpretation.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzed a stratified sample of 5,400 primary and secondary school teachers in China, using questionnaire measures of teacher stress (22 items across six stress factors including workload, student academics, social/school evaluation, professional development, student problem behavior, and technology stress), emotional labor (surface acting, deep acting, expression of naturally felt emotions), burnout (7 items), work engagement (6 items on a 7-point scale), and school support (8 items on a 7-point scale). The authors estimated relationships using structural equation modeling in SPSS/AMOS/Mplus, reporting model fit for the mediation model (CFI=0.842, RMSEA=0.084, PNFI=0.774). Teacher stress significantly predicted lower work engagement (β=-0.316, p<.01), with mediation through burnout (indirect β=-0.247, p<.01) and a chained pathway involving surface acting and burnout (indirect β=-0.038, p<.01). School support also showed significant associations with emotional labor, burnout, and work engagement, but the manuscript does not report any missing-data handling strategy and the design is cross-sectional self-report, limiting causal claims.
